name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
objectives: Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
approach: To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated.

key_findings.text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.

key_findings.text: Burning on flat plates was studied at various orientations with respect to gravity. Flat wicks of ceramic (Kaowool PM) board (10 cm wide and 1–10 cm long) were saturated with methanol or ethanol. Steady flames were obtained that ranged from boundary layer flames to plume-type burning. The onset of unsteady flow and transition to turbulence commenced at Grashof numbers of 10 6 –10 7 , increasing with decreasing angle (toward underside burning).

key_findings.text: The burning rate emulator (BRE) is a burner that emulates condensed fuel flames using gaseous fuel/inert mixtures by matching four properties: the heat of combustion; the heat of gasification; the laminar smoke point; and the surface temperature. Matching the heat of gasification requires measuring the burner heat flux, for which the BRE has embedded heat flux gauges and a copper top‐plate calorimeter.

ignition_findings.text: Astronauts observed unique transient phenomena during ignition and near extinction that were not visible from ground observations.
The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.
At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s. Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly.

Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2, a sustained ignition could not be achieved even though flames were observed when the igniter was on and briefly after the igniter was turned off before extinguishing.
Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached.
Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition.
The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.

A thick PMMA slab will take time to ignite and grow to a steady-state size, and the sample burning rate distribution is an important quantity to determine how much heat is being generated by the flame.
Solid fuel ignition uses a Kanthal hot wire.
In the event of a non-ignition of the rod at low O2, an opposed ignition will be attempted, followed by an ambient air opposed or concurrent test.

flame_spread_findings.text: At higher opposed-flow velocities, the flame spread rate is inversely proportional to fuel thickness and independent of the flow velocity, consistent with thermal theory.
In the microgravity regime, the flame spread rate decreases as the opposed-flow velocity is reduced, eventually leading to extinction.
the spread rate is independent of opposing flow velocity Vg for thin fuels while it is proportional to Vg for thick fuels.
the average flame spread rate increases with opposed-flow velocity, even within the small range of flow velocities tested.
Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments
Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.
The flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue shape just before quenching.

Gas sensor data and rod mass loss estimates indicate that the flames are globally stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations but become more globally fuel rich as the minimum O2 concentration is approached.
CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels. The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations.

In Figure D.6, a one-sided PMMA slab was burned at a slow flow. The 1-cm-wide sample took 7.5 min for the total test time, with the ignition taking over 1 min. Flame reached steady size in about 3 min and was only 15 mm long. The spread rate was 0.037 mm/s (0.0037 cm/s or 2.2 mm/min).
Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

extinction_findings.text: The critical flow velocity required to prevent radiative extinction is independent of the fuel thickness.
The critical extinction velocity increases significantly as the ambient oxygen concentration is reduced.
A simplified scale analysis was developed to predict the critical extinction velocity, showing good agreement with experimental and computational results.
At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.
While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out.
Prequenching extinction oscillations at 1.1 Hz are observed with a radiometer and are similar to previously reported quiescent candle flame oscillations in microgravity.
As flow speed is increased, blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.

Once the stagnation region is blown far enough downstream of the stagnation region (greater than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ), the flame is unable to propagate back upstream even when the flow is reduced.
In the quenching region, surface radiative loss dominates. Solid conductive loss down the rod is lower and decreases with decreasing stretch due to the low Peclet number.
Quenching flow velocities were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher velocity at lower O2 percentage.

As the quenching limit is approached (in this case by turning down the flow velocity), the fuel pyrolysis rate and combustion heat release rate (HRR) are reduced, and radiation loss becomes a significant fraction of the HRR from the shrinking flame. When the flame becomes small enough, conduction becomes the additional heat loss.
Brief ignition but flame extinguished before spreading beyond igniter
Extinction is observed for tests that seek to find a flammability limit.
Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed.

key_findings.text: The BASS-II experiments successfully utilized nitrogen dilution in the Microgravity Science Glovebox to study solid fuel combustion at reduced oxygen levels.
The global equivalence ratio for the tests was estimated to be fuel-rich, averaging 1.3, indicating under-ventilated combustion.
Heat release rates calculated from oxygen consumption were generally below 100 W for most of the tests.

flame_spread_findings.text: For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed.

In the concurrent-flow configuration, flame size grew with time during the tests. A limiting length and steady spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds (<= 10 cm/s) for the short-length samples that fit in the small wind tunnel.
For concurrent flow, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow.
Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds.
The concurrent-flow flame is longer and spreads twice as fast as the opposed-flow flame at 10 cm/s air flow speed.

extinction_findings.text: By decreasing concurrent-flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.
Based on the trends, it appears that an opposed-flow quenching extinction limit can be extrapolated to exist at an air flow speed of less than 1 cm/s.
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.

key_findings.text: These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).
Materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity with all other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.).
The custom-made cotton-fiberglass fabric performed very well, with none of the complications caused by the burnout of ordinary cellulosic fuel samples like paper.
This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity for a thin fuel with uniform burnout characteristics.

fire_safety_relevance: BASS results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. It helps bridge the gap between normal gravity material screening tests (like NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) and actual flammability in microgravity, where materials may burn more readily due to low-speed ventilation.

approach: The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.

approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI. The procedure involves selecting test pressures (0.5 - 1.5 atm), droplet sizes (~3 mm), and ambient oxygen mole fractions, performing droplet combustion tests, and iteratively adjusting droplet size and oxygen concentration to map flammability boundaries. For slow flow tests, droplets are subjected to a small, sub-buoyant convective flow near the end of the test to examine its influence on extinction.

flame_spread_findings.text: After considering measurement uncertainties, burning rates decreased appreciably as the initial droplet diameter increased for combustion in air but not for combustion in the oxygen/helium environments.

evidence.title: Combustion of Submillimeter Heptane/Methanol and Heptane/Ethanol Droplets in Reduced Gravity

flame_spread_findings.text: Addition of either methanol or ethanol did not influence burning rates appreciably and burning rates were larger for the oxygen/helium environments than for air if initial droplet diameter dependences were accounted for.

evidence.title: Combustion of Submillimeter Heptane/Methanol and Heptane/Ethanol Droplets in Reduced Gravity

flame_spread_findings.text: Burning rates were about 40% to 70% higher in normal gravity than in reduced gravity.

evidence.title: Combustion of Methanol Droplets in Air-Diluent Environments with Reduced and Normal Gravity

flame_spread_findings.text: Methanol droplets had burning rates that were typically larger than 1-propanol burning rates by about 20% in reduced gravity, whereas in normal gravity, burning rate differences between the two fuels were significantly smaller.

evidence.title: Combustion of Methanol Droplets in Air-Diluent Environments with Reduced and Normal Gravity

extinction_findings.text: In reduced gravity, droplets would burn steadily with a xenon mole fraction of 0.50 but would not burn steadily if helium or carbon dioxide mole fractions were 0.50.

evidence.title: Combustion of Methanol Droplets in Air-Diluent Environments with Reduced and Normal Gravity

key_findings.text: Ambient gas transport properties play an important role in determining flammability and combustion behaviors including burning rates and radiant heat output histories of the droplets.

evidence.title: Combustion of Methanol Droplets in Air-Diluent Environments with Reduced and Normal Gravity

key_findings.text: When a laminar diffusion flame is established over a spinning, thermoplastic, polymer fuel disc in a quiescent, oxidizing environment, the polymer melts and flows radially outwards, causing some fuel to be lost and not transported to the diffusion flame.

evidence.title: Analysis of the melt phase of a rotating polymer disc supporting a diffusion flame

fire_safety_relevance: By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
objectives: determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity
investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.

Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.

name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
objectives: Characterize the smoke aerosol encountered in space vehicles using the moment method in conjunction with the lognormal distribution assumption
Identify particle size distributions of aerosol produced from five tested materials commonly found in spacecraft
Examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials
make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors
Quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment

Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging
Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison
Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test conditions
Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials
approach: The experiment utilized the SAME hardware already on orbit with reloaded sample carousels, rebuilt thermal precipitators, and refilled alcohol cartridge. It heated samples of various materials (Teflon, Kapton, Pyrell, silicone rubber, cellulose/lamp wick) under different temperatures and air flow rates, and measured the resulting smoke aerosol using moment instruments (P-trak, DustTrak, MPASS) and collected samples on TEM grids.

key_findings.text: Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles.

The comparatively much smaller diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system.
It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.

The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume.
Silicone particles were not wholly preserved on the TEM grids owing to the volatile nature of the pyrolysis products.
Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols so they are better suited to the moment method.
Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles.
The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diameters, with the increase in the count mean diameter being greater than the corresponding increase in the diameter of average mass.
Particle diameters for Teflon, Kapton, and lampwick show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates.
For all of the materials, the diameter of average mass is 30% to 40% larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.
The zero-flow condition changed the morphology of Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres (at 8 cm/s flow) to spherical particles.

fire_safety_relevance: The larger particle diameters observed in zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles.

name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
objectives: characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety of overheated spacecraft materials
obtain this data that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration missions
To make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.
Quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the Μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging.
Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison.
Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test conditions.
Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials
approach: The moment method was developed, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a minimum number of portable instruments. Samples of materials were heated to temperatures below the ignition point under controlled repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The transport time was simulated by holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis, and smoke properties were measured using particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different moments of the size distribution.
